decisions.quote: We randomized the groups’ response to five different political statements and find an average conformity rate of 38%. Hence, these results suggest that the original finding of Asch can also be generalized to matters of opinion. This result is in line with former evidence by Crutchfield [ 8 ], and Mallinson and Hatemi [ 9 ]. However, both of these studies had only small sample sizes of 50 and 58 subjects respectively, which called for further replication studies. Finally, we measured the Big Five, intelligence, self-esteem and social approval. With the exception of openness, our study finds no support that these personality traits are statistically significantly related to the susceptibility of group pressure.
decisions.reason: Although framed as an extension relative to Asch's line task, the paper directly re-tests Crutchfield's (1955) published findings on political-opinion conformity (H3, derived in Section 2.2 from Crutchfield's 36-40 percentage-point effects with n=50) and individual-difference correlates of conformity (intellectual competence, self-esteem/ego strength, and need for social approval in Section 2.3, H4-H6) in a larger sample (N=202). The Conclusion explicitly states that Crutchfield's small sample size called for further replication studies and confirms the political-opinion conformity effect (38%), while finding no overall support for the intelligence, self-esteem, and social-approval associations, yielding a mixed outcome.

decisions.location: Section 2.3 Individual differences (line 109, chunk 21); Section 4 Results (line 153)
decisions.quote: Crutchfield [ 8 ] studied the effect of intellectual competence on conformity. He found that higher competence was associated with lower levels of conformity. However, intelligence was measured by the subjective ratings of the experimental staff. Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey [ 10 ] exposed high school students (7 to 15 years) to group pressure in an acoustic task (counting metronome ticks), and approximated intelligence by subjects’ school records. They found no correlation of school records with conformity. Uchida et al. [ 31 ] studied 12 to 14 year-old high school students and assessed scholastic achievements by their school performance. They report that high achievers conformed less to the majority than low achievers. Hence, results of the effect of intelligence on conformity are inconclusive so far and the existing studies use indirect measures (school grades) but do not measure intelligence directly.
decisions.reason: The current paper explicitly treats Uchida et al. scholastic achievement as an indirect intelligence measure motivating H5, and tests a negative fluid-intelligence/conformity association. The complete original does report an overall high-/low-achievement conformity difference, as well as conditional minority/majority status effects; it is therefore too strong to exclude it merely because no IQ test or peer-status manipulation is repeated. Yet the original operationalises attained school achievement and hypothesised status/confidence, while the current regression operationalises adult matrix intelligence without achievement or group status. The current source supplies no original-specific results comparison resolving whether this is an empirical conceptual retest of that attainment finding or a new latent-cognitive claim prompted by the literature. This is a genuine construct/finding correspondence ambiguity in two available complete reports, not an original access limit and not a methods-difference exclusion. Original-only group-composition findings are not transferred.

decisions.location: Section 5 Conclusion and discussion (chunk 45); see also Section 2.1 Monetary incentives (chunks 14-16) and Reference 5 (chunk 52)
decisions.quote: In this study we first replicated the original experiment of Asch [ 1 – 3 ] with 5 confederates and ten line tasks. We find an average error rate of 33% which replicates the original findings of Asch very closely and which is in line with other replications that were conducted predominately with American students [ 12 ]. Together with recent studies from Japan [ 14 ], and Bosnia and Herzegowina [ 15 ], our study provides further evidence that the influence of groups on individuals’ judgments is a universal phenomenon, and is still valid today. Furthermore, we incentivized the decisions and find a drop of the error rate by 8%-points to 25%. Hence, monetary incentives do not eliminate the effect of group pressure. This finding sheds doubt on former results which predominately show the opposite effect, namely that incentives increase compliance [ 5 ,  6 ].
decisions.reason: Section 2.1 reviews Baron et al. [5] (1996) on monetary incentives in conformity (decreasing conformity by half to 15% on easy eyewitness tasks but increasing compliance on difficult tasks), notes its small sample size, and derives H2 (rewards for nonconformity decrease group pressure). Franzen and Mader (2023) empirically test randomized piece-rate monetary incentives (1 CHF per correct line judgment, n=103 vs n=99) across easy and hard critical trials (Fig 1), finding an 8%-point reduction in conformity to 25%, and explicitly contrast this outcome in Section 5 against [5, 6] as shedding doubt on former results showing that incentives increase compliance. Although the current study uses an Asch line task and does not re-estimate a formal reward-by-difficulty interaction term, this is a direct conceptual empirical retest and explicit results comparison against Baron et al.'s (1996) directional incentive claim. Baron et al. (1996) is absent from shipped row 6 (Asch, 1956) and sibling targets.
